claims.text: Daily social media hours were not significantly correlated with sleep duration in the synthetic dataset (r = -0.009, p = .743).
Screen time before sleep was not significantly correlated with sleep duration in the synthetic dataset (r = .010, p = .723).
Daily social media hours were not significantly correlated with anxiety level in the synthetic dataset (r = .028, p = .335).
Daily social media hours were not significantly correlated with stress level in the synthetic dataset (r = .031, p = .288).

A multiple linear regression model predicting sleep duration from daily social media hours, screen time before sleep, age, gender, and physical activity explained almost none of the variance (R² = .001, p = .895).
Mean sleep duration did not differ significantly across quartile-based daily social media usage groups (F(3, 1196) = 1.10, p = .348, η² = .003).
In the synthetic dataset, records labeled with depression had significantly lower mean sleep duration than records without the depression label (t(40.99) = -15.75, p < .001, Cohen's d = -1.22).
Sleep duration was negatively correlated with the synthetic depression label (r = -.191, p < .001), while daily social media use was positively correlated with it (r = .175, p < .001).

evidence.description: Pearson correlation between daily social media hours and sleep duration was r = −.009, p = .743, 95% CI [−.066, .047] across 1,200 records.
Pearson correlation between screen time before sleep and sleep duration was r = .010, p = .723, 95% CI [−.046, .067].
Pearson correlation between daily social media hours and anxiety level was r = .028, p = .335, 95% CI [−.029, .084].
Pearson correlation between daily social media hours and stress level was r = .031, p = .288, 95% CI [−.026, .087].

Multiple regression predicting sleep duration gave F(5, 1194) = 0.33, p = .895, R² = .001, adjusted R² = −.003, with daily social media use (B = -0.007, p = .735) and screen time before sleep (B = 0.020, p = .730).
One-way ANOVA across four quartile groups showed mean sleep hours between 6.36 and 6.54 hours, F(3, 1196) = 1.10, p = .348, η² = .003.

Welch independent-samples t test showed records labeled 1 had lower mean sleep duration (M = 4.76, SD = 0.57, n = 31) than records labeled 0 (M = 6.49, SD = 1.43, n = 1,169), t(40.99) = −15.75, p < .001, Cohen's d = −1.22.
Point-biserial correlations showed sleep duration r = -.191, p < .001 and daily social media use r = .175, p < .001 with the binary depression label.

methodologies.name: Correlational analysis with Bonferroni correction
methodologies.description: Calculated Pearson correlation coefficients with Bonferroni-adjusted alpha of .0125 to test four primary hypotheses regarding screen use, sleep duration, anxiety, and stress.
conditions: Two-tailed t-distribution with N - 2 degrees of freedom

methodologies.name: Multiple linear regression and one-way ANOVA
methodologies.description: Regressed sleep duration onto daily social media hours, screen time before sleep, age, gender, and physical activity, and conducted a one-way ANOVA across quartile-based social media usage groups.
conditions: Predictors: daily social media use, screen time before sleep, age, female gender dummy, physical activity

limitations.text: The data were artificially generated and did not come from real adolescents, meaning results cannot be generalized to real adolescents.
The dataset documentation does not explain how anxiety, stress, addiction, and social interaction were measured, nor are they documented as validated instruments.
The binary depression label is neither explained nor validated as a clinical measure, and suffers from severe class imbalance (only 31 of 1,200 records labeled 1).
The dataset provides information at only one point in time and cannot determine temporal changes or causal relationships.
Most existing studies on social media and youth mental health are correlational and rely on self-reported data, making it difficult to establish whether social media directly causes these outcomes.

future_work.text: Test nonlinear patterns and interaction effects among social media use, pre-bedtime screen use, addiction, and social interaction, and examine stability under alternative grouping methods.
Collect real longitudinal adolescent data with validated psychological measures to evaluate adolescent well-being.
